front: The lesson names four treatments that all aimed to remove an excess humour. Name all four.
answer: Bleeding (phlebotomy) / Purging with laxatives / Sweating in hot baths / Cupping with heated jars
title: Medieval Medicine: Humours, Galen and the Doctor's World

front: Below the university-trained physician, three other kinds of healer treated ordinary people. Name all three.
answer: Barber-surgeons / Apothecaries / Wise women
title: Medieval Medicine: Humours, Galen and the Doctor's World

front: Why did a medieval doctor bleed a patient who had a fever?
answer: A fever was thought to mean too much blood, so taking blood away would bring the four humours back into balance.
title: Medieval Medicine: Humours, Galen and the Doctor's World

front: How did a medieval dissection end up confirming Galen instead of testing him?
answer: The physician read Galen aloud while a barber-surgeon cut, so when the body did not match the book the body was called abnormal.
title: Medieval Medicine: Humours, Galen and the Doctor's World

front: Name the five operations the lesson says medieval barber-surgeons carried out.
answer: Setting broken bones / Removing arrowheads / Cauterising wounds with a hot iron / Treating boils / Trepanning the skull
items: Cauterising wounds with a hot iron
title: The Church, the Monastery and Islamic Medicine

front: The lesson gives three ways the medieval Church helped medicine. Name all three.
answer: Built hospitals / Copied classical medical texts / Trained literate physicians
title: The Church, the Monastery and Islamic Medicine

front: Why could a medieval doctor who doubted Galen not prove him wrong?
answer: The 1163 Council of Tours banned clergy from cutting open bodies, so dissection stayed rare and there was no way to test Galen.
title: The Church, the Monastery and Islamic Medicine

front: Why were Hugh and Theodoric of Lucca centuries ahead of other surgeons?
answer: They argued in the thirteenth century that wounds healed better kept clean, against the common view that pus was a healthy sign.
title: The Church, the Monastery and Islamic Medicine

front: London's town rules in the 1300s did three things to keep the streets cleaner. Name all three.
answer: Butchers slaughtered outside the walls / Fines for letting pigs run loose / Rakers paid to clear streets
items: Fines for letting pigs run loose
title: Public Health in the Middle Ages and the Black Death

front: Name the four religious responses to the Black Death that the lesson gives.
answer: Prayer / Processions / Wearing crosses / Flagellants whipping themselves
title: Public Health in the Middle Ages and the Black Death

front: How did the Black Death give surviving workers more bargaining power?
answer: So many people died that workers were scarce, so survivors could demand higher wages and gradually move off the land.
title: Public Health in the Middle Ages and the Black Death

front: Why did cesspits make people ill in crowded medieval parishes?
answer: Cesspits were dug in back gardens, and in dense parishes one building's cesspit leaked into the well another household drank from.
title: Public Health in the Middle Ages and the Black Death

front: The lesson gives three mistakes of Galen's that Vesalius corrected. Name all three.
answer: The jaw is one bone / The breastbone has three sections / The heart wall has no holes
items: The heart wall has no holes
title: Renaissance Anatomy: Vesalius, Paré and the Challenge to Galen

front: Galen had only ever dissected animals. Name the three the lesson lists.
answer: Apes / Pigs / Dogs
title: Renaissance Anatomy: Vesalius, Paré and the Challenge to Galen

front: How did Paré find out that boiling oil was the wrong treatment for gunshot wounds?
answer: He ran out of oil, dressed the rest with a cool salve, and next morning those men were calmer and less inflamed.
title: Renaissance Anatomy: Vesalius, Paré and the Challenge to Galen

front: Why did Vesalius's corrections not change how British patients were treated?
answer: Treatment still followed the four humours, so knowing the heart had no holes told a physician nothing new to do for a fever.
title: Renaissance Anatomy: Vesalius, Paré and the Challenge to Galen

front: Four developments anchor British medicine between about 1600 and 1750. Name all four.
answer: Harvey on circulation / Sydenham's clinical observation / The rise of voluntary hospitals / Hunter's scientific surgery
title: Harvey, Sydenham and Disease Treatment c1600-1750

front: Name the three voluntary hospitals the lesson gives, with the year each opened.
answer: Westminster, 1719 / Guy's, 1724 / The London, 1740
title: Harvey, Sydenham and Disease Treatment c1600-1750

front: Why did Harvey's proof of circulation make bleeding look pointless?
answer: If blood moves in a continuous loop rather than being used up, removing pints of it weakens the patient instead of rebalancing him.
title: Harvey, Sydenham and Disease Treatment c1600-1750

front: Why does the Great Plague of 1665 show how little had changed since 1348?
answer: The response was the same, with quarantine, herb-stuffed masks against miasma, prayer and street cleaning, because nothing had been learned about the cause.
title: Harvey, Sydenham and Disease Treatment c1600-1750

front: Opposition to vaccination came from three directions. Name all three.
answer: Inoculators losing their business / Clergy objecting to beast matter / Ordinary people fearing something new
title: Jenner, Vaccination and the Limits of 18th-Century Prevention

front: Name the three Vaccination Acts the lesson gives and what each one did.
answer: 1853 — vaccination made compulsory / 1871 — local Vaccination Officers / 1898 — conscience clause added
title: Jenner, Vaccination and the Limits of 18th-Century Prevention

front: Why was inoculation out of reach for most families?
answer: It cost around £5 a child, about a labourer's monthly wage, so only people who could pay were protected.
title: Jenner, Vaccination and the Limits of 18th-Century Prevention

front: Why is Jenner credited with vaccination when Benjamin Jesty had used cowpox first?
answer: Jesty inoculated his own family in 1774, but Jenner was the first to test the idea systematically, record the cases and publish them.
title: Jenner, Vaccination and the Limits of 18th-Century Prevention

front: Name the three diseases Pasteur made vaccines for, with the year of each.
answer: Chicken cholera, 1879 / Anthrax, 1881 / Rabies, 1885
title: Pasteur, Koch and the Germ Theory Revolution

front: Doctors still prescribed three traditional remedies in the age of germ theory. Name all three.
answer: Cod liver oil / Beef tea / Mustard plasters
title: Pasteur, Koch and the Germ Theory Revolution

front: Why did miasma theory keep its hold even though it was wrong?
answer: It was coherent, predicting that clean smells meant safety and dirty smells danger, and it produced useful action such as ventilation and street cleaning.
title: Pasteur, Koch and the Germ Theory Revolution

front: How did Koch's work lead Ehrlich to the idea of a magic bullet?
answer: If one particular germ caused one particular disease, then one particular chemical might destroy that germ without harming the patient.
title: Pasteur, Koch and the Germ Theory Revolution

front: Name the three early anaesthetics the lesson gives, with who used each and when.
answer: Nitrous oxide — Davy, 1799 / Ether — Morton, 1846 / Chloroform — Simpson, 1847
title: A Revolution in Surgery: Anaesthetics and Antiseptics

front: Name the four things aseptic surgery added by the 1890s.
answer: Steam autoclaves for instruments / Surgical gowns and face masks / Scrubbing hands before operating / Rubber gloves
title: A Revolution in Surgery: Anaesthetics and Antiseptics

front: How did Pasteur's germ theory lead Lister to carbolic acid?
answer: Lister read the theory in 1864 and reasoned that if germs in the air caused decay, they must also be infecting open wounds.
title: A Revolution in Surgery: Anaesthetics and Antiseptics

front: Why did Halsted introduce rubber gloves in 1889?
answer: The antiseptics used in his operating theatre had cracked his nurse's hands, so he had rubber gloves made for her.
title: A Revolution in Surgery: Anaesthetics and Antiseptics

front: Name the four major cholera epidemics of nineteenth-century Britain by their years.
title: Public Health in the Industrial City: Snow, Chadwick and the Acts

front: The 1875 Public Health Act made local authorities responsible for five things. Name them.
answer: Sewers / Water / Food / Housing / Notifiable disease
title: Public Health in the Industrial City: Snow, Chadwick and the Acts
problems: the set is not closed in the lesson

front: Why did the medical establishment reject Snow's finding about the Broad Street pump?
answer: The General Board of Health still preferred miasma, and his evidence was only accepted once germ theory caught up in the 1860s.
title: Public Health in the Industrial City: Snow, Chadwick and the Acts

front: How did laissez-faire hold back public health in the industrial city?
answer: It held that the state should leave people and businesses alone, so government would not make towns build sewers or supply clean water.
title: Public Health in the Industrial City: Snow, Chadwick and the Acts

front: Nightingale insisted on five things at Scutari. Name all five.
answer: Cleanliness / Ventilation / Separating patients by disease / Decent food / Proper laundry
title: Nightingale, Hospitals and the Reform of Nursing

front: Notes on Nursing set out six things a trained nurse must manage. Name them.
answer: Observation / Hygiene / Ventilation / Diet / Quiet / Light
title: Nightingale, Hospitals and the Reform of Nursing

front: Why did the pavilion plan cut infection before germ theory explained why?
answer: Long wards with windows on both sides and separate buildings for each disease kept air moving and stopped patients infecting one another.
title: Nightingale, Hospitals and the Reform of Nursing

front: Why did Mary Seacole get far less recognition than Nightingale?
answer: She paid her own way after the War Office refused her, and race, class and political contacts decided which reformers became household names.
title: Nightingale, Hospitals and the Reform of Nursing

front: The lesson names four pressures that pushed the state into welfare. Name all four.
answer: Booth's London survey / Rowntree's York study / The Boer War recruit rejections / The 1906 Liberal landslide
title: From Booth and Rowntree to the Liberal Reforms 1900-1914

front: The Liberal reforms faced opposition from four directions. Name all four.
answer: The British Medical Association / Conservatives in the Lords / Friendly societies / The Labour Party
title: From Booth and Rowntree to the Liberal Reforms 1900-1914

front: How did the Boer War change the argument for helping the poor?
answer: About 40% of volunteers were rejected as unfit, so welfare became a question of national security rather than of compassion.
title: From Booth and Rowntree to the Liberal Reforms 1900-1914

front: Why did Booth and Rowntree change middle-class minds about poverty?
answer: Their surveys found 30.7% of Londoners and 28% of York below the poverty line, so poverty could no longer be blamed on idleness.
title: From Booth and Rowntree to the Liberal Reforms 1900-1914

front: The penicillin story needed four things to come together. Name all four.
answer: Chance — Fleming's contaminated plate / The individual — Florey and Chain / Science — deep-tank fermentation / War — wartime demand and funding
title: Penicillin, Modern Surgery and the Wars

front: Name the four developments that reshaped surgery after 1945.
answer: Heart transplants, 1967 / Keyhole surgery from the 1980s / Laser surgery / Radiotherapy
title: Penicillin, Modern Surgery and the Wars

front: Why did penicillin sit unused for ten years after 1928?
answer: Fleming could not purify it in useful quantities, so it stayed a laboratory observation in the journals until Florey and Chain took it up.
title: Penicillin, Modern Surgery and the Wars

front: How did superbugs such as MRSA appear in hospitals?
answer: Antibiotics were over-prescribed, so bacteria evolved resistance, and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus emerged in the 1960s.
title: Penicillin, Modern Surgery and the Wars

front: Name Beveridge's five giants on the road to reconstruction.
answer: Want / Disease / Ignorance / Squalor / Idleness
title: Beveridge, Bevan and the Birth of the NHS

front: Name the five things every resident got free when the health service opened.
answer: A registered GP / Hospital treatment / Dental care / Eye tests / Prescriptions
title: Beveridge, Bevan and the Birth of the NHS

front: How did the Second World War change what people expected the state to do?
answer: Evacuation exposed city children's poverty, rationing improved working-class diet, and the Emergency Medical Service put every hospital bed under central government.
title: Beveridge, Bevan and the Birth of the NHS

front: Why did demand beat every Treasury forecast in the first year?
answer: People who had never been able to afford care came forward, taking 8.5 million pairs of glasses and dental treatment in twelve months.
title: Beveridge, Bevan and the Birth of the NHS

front: Name the four wars the lesson says sped up medical change, and what each brought.
answer: Crimean — Nightingale's nursing reform / Boer — the Liberal reforms / First World War — transfusion, X-rays / Second World War — penicillin, the NHS
items: Second World War — penicillin, the NHS
title: Weighing the Factors: Continuity, Change and Progress c1000-Today

front: Name the three chance discoveries the lesson compares across the periods.
answer: Paré's salve / Pasteur's chicken-cholera culture / Fleming's mould
title: Weighing the Factors: Continuity, Change and Progress c1000-Today

front: Why can the same medical change be progress for some people and not for others?
answer: What lengthens life may not give patients more choice, and what improves health overall can still leave particular groups worse off.
title: Weighing the Factors: Continuity, Change and Progress c1000-Today

front: Why could government not have improved public health on its own?
answer: Without Pasteur, Koch and Snow the 1875 Act would have been a shot in the dark, and individuals turned those findings into law.
title: Weighing the Factors: Continuity, Change and Progress c1000-Today
